units.text: Follow the orange query in the left panel. The client asks the VPC Resolver for a name, and receives the example private address shown by the blue return arrow.
Move to the right panel. The application connection is a separate step to the returned address. Routes, security groups and network ACLs still determine whether that connection can succeed.
Read the three lower callouts. A valid DNS answer does not prove application connectivity, and a cached answer can continue to be used until its time to live expires.
With the whole slide visible, troubleshoot the name, returned address, network path and application separately. DNS supplies an answer; it is not an application traffic forwarding hop.
Start at the client on the left and follow the first arrow to the recursive resolver. The client asks for a record, while the resolver can return an eligible cached response.

Follow the purple arrows on the right. When the answer is not cached, resolution obtains authoritative records, then returns a response to the client. The diagram summarizes the roles rather than every possible delegation step.

Read the positive and negative cache panels below. Successful records and some negative responses can be cached under DNS rules. Changing an authoritative record does not flush existing client or resolver caches.

With the original slide fully visible, identify which resolver and cache supplied the answer before changing a record. Treat the displayed addresses and time to live as examples, not a claim about current public records.
Compare the two panels. An internet client uses the public DNS view, while a client using the VPC Resolver can use a private hosted zone associated with its VPC.

Follow the public path on the left. The zone needs correct delegation, and its record identifies the public application entry. The diagram shows DNS selection, not application packets traveling through the hosted zone.

Now follow the private path and its lower callouts. Associate the private zone with the VPC and enable the required DNS settings. A matching private namespace does not automatically fall back to public DNS when the requested record is absent.

With both views visible, compare the caller's resolver, zone association and requested record type before comparing answers. The same name can intentionally select different application endpoints in the public and private views.
